text: The hardest ML incidents aren't the loud ones. They're the ones where everything looks healthy and the model is quietly making worse decisions anyway. Let's walk through exactly that, start to finish.

Every incident moves through the same four stages. Detect — an alert fires, or a human notices first. Triage — figure out what's actually happening before touching anything. Mitigate — stop the damage now, even if it's not the permanent fix. And postmortem — write down what happened and why, blamelessly, once things are stable.

Here's the scenario. The fraud team messages the platform team, not a page: approval rate for one customer segment dropped eight percent over four days. Every SLO from lesson thirty-one is green — no errors, no latency spike, features arriving right on schedule. The service is healthy. The model isn't. On triage, a feature is fresh, but not right — an upstream service quietly changed how it buckets account ages, and the feature's values no longer mean what the model was trained on.

Instead of guessing, the on-call engineer runs a population stability index check, comparing the feature's training-time distribution against the last forty eight hours of production traffic. A score above point two confirms it: this feature has shifted enough to plausibly explain the whole drop. Triage is done — the cause is confirmed, not just suspected.

With the cause confirmed, there are real options, fastest first. A feature killswitch falls back to a safe default without touching the model at all. Rolling back to a model version less sensitive to this feature uses the registry and rollback paths from chapter five. Or fail over this segment to a conservative rule for a short window. None of these is retraining — that happens deliberately, later, not mid-incident.

Once the killswitch is in and approval rate recovers, the postmortem matters as much as the fix. It stays blameless — contributing causes, not individual fault — with a specific timeline and root cause. And it ends in action items with owners: what was a one-off Python script during this incident becomes a standing, automated SLO the next time lesson thirty-one's config gets updated.

Silent degradation, confirmed by distribution, mitigated fast, closed out with a blameless postmortem that becomes a standing safeguard. Up next, the course's capstone: lesson thirty-four asks you to design a platform that handles all of this, from scratch, for a team scaling past fifteen models.
